summary: Specifies the Voucher Trading System Application Programming Interface (VTS-API). It lets a wallet or other application issue, transfer and redeem vouchers uniformly, independent of the underlying VTS implementation. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a set of buttons for a digital wallet: give out a coupon, hand one to a friend, or use one. The buttons look the same no matter how the machine behind them works.

subtitle: A uniform interface for digital wallets to issue, transfer and redeem vouchers.

tldr.problem: Digital wallets and payment systems need a standard way to handle vouchers, coupons and similar digital assets across different backend implementations.
tldr.mechanism: VTS-API defines a set of Java interfaces that applications can use to issue, transfer, consume and redeem vouchers in a uniform way, independent of whether the voucher system is centralized online or distributed across smartcards.
tldr.outcome: Applications can work with any VTS implementation that follows the API, without needing to know how that implementation stores or manages vouchers internally.

today: RFC 4154 is an Informational RFC from 2005 and has not been obsoleted. It remains available for implementation by wallet and voucher system developers.

sections.title: Overview of the Voucher Trading System API
sections.content:
RFC 4154 specifies the Voucher Trading System Application Programming Interface (VTS-API), a set of standard interfaces for building software that manages digital vouchers. The API lets wallet applications, issuers and collectors handle vouchers such as coupons, tickets, loyalty points and gift certificates in a uniform way.

The key innovation is that the API works with both centralized VTS implementations, where a server manages all vouchers in a database, and distributed implementations, where vouchers are stored on individual smartcards. This means developers can write one application that works with any VTS backend without modification.
sections.eli5: The API is like a universal plug that works in any country's socket. Whether the voucher system is online or on a card, your wallet app talks to it the same way.

sections.title: The Modular Wallet Architecture
sections.content:
The VTS-API assumes a modular wallet architecture where different VTS systems can be added as plug-ins to a wallet application. Rather than defining the protocol that VTS plug-ins use internally (which varies by implementation), the API defines the common interface that applications use to call the plug-in.

This separation allows a single application to support multiple VTS implementations. For example, a wallet can include one plug-in for centralized bank vouchers and another for smartcard-based store loyalty programs. The application calls the same API methods on each plug-in, but the plug-ins handle the specifics of their own VTS implementation.

The document assumes that voucher content is described using the separate Generic Voucher Language (GVL), an XML-based format that specifies what each voucher represents and what it can be redeemed for.
sections.eli5: Your wallet has slot for different plug-ins, like cartridges for a game console. Each plug-in talks to a different store system, but they all plug in the same way.

sections.title: The Core Interfaces
sections.content:
The VTS-API defines nine main interfaces. At the top level, VTSManager is the entry point that provides access to two repositories: a ParticipantRepository (an address book of trading partners) and a VoucherComponentRepository (a registry of voucher types).

The VTSAgent is the central interface for voucher operations. Each VTSAgent is associated with a participant (a user, issuer or collector) and provides methods to issue, transfer, consume, present and delete vouchers. Before calling any of these methods, an application must call login() to authenticate, then prepare() to establish a Session with a specific trading partner.

A Session represents an ongoing voucher transaction and tracks its state through four stages: prepared (ready to start), activated (transaction in progress), suspended (paused due to error) and completed (finished). The Voucher interface represents one or more vouchers with the same issuer and promise. The ReceptionListener interface lets applications be notified when vouchers arrive.
sections.eli5: You open the wallet app (VTSManager), pick a friend from your contacts (Participant), start a handshake with them (Session), then hand them a coupon (Voucher).

sections.title: The Four Core Trading Operations
sections.content:
The VTS-API defines four main ways to move vouchers between participants:

Issue: An issuer creates new vouchers and sends them to a holder. For example, a store issues a discount coupon.

Transfer: A holder moves vouchers they own to another participant. For example, you send a loyalty point to a friend.

Consume: A holder sends vouchers to a collector and those vouchers are deleted (redeemed). For example, you redeem a coupon at checkout.

Present: A holder proves to another party that they own vouchers without deleting them. For example, you show that you have frequent-buyer status without using up the points.

All four operations follow the same pattern: call prepare() to set up a session with the other party, then call the operation method with the session, the voucher issuer, the voucher type and the number of vouchers. The session's state then moves to activated, and either completes successfully or suspends if the network fails. Suspended sessions can be resumed later by calling resume().
sections.eli5: Issue is giving someone a coupon. Transfer is passing it to a friend. Consume is using it and throwing it away. Present is showing you have it without using it up.

sections.title: Authentication and Trust Considerations
sections.content:
The VTS-API requires authentication before any voucher operation. The login() method takes a passphrase, though for smartcard-based implementations the authentication can happen without user input, for example by asking the smartcard to respond to a cryptographic challenge from the server.

The RFC notes that VTS implementations are responsible for preventing voucher fraud such as forgery or duplication. In a centralized implementation, this is typically done through database transactions with access controls. In a distributed implementation, it uses cryptographic protocols to verify the validity of each voucher.

The RFC explicitly states an important limitation: the API itself does not specify how an application should authenticate the VTS plug-in itself. Applications must verify that the VTS software they are using comes from a trusted source and securely bind it to the voucher provider information specified in the voucher component. This is typically done by verifying digital signatures on the plug-in before loading it.
sections.eli5: The wallet checks that you are who you say you are. The voucher system checks that vouchers are real and haven't been copied. But you also need to make sure the wallet app itself is genuine.
